templates.name: Period between independent clauses (second often opens with an introductory phrase)
Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
Dash pair around a supplementary element
Items in a series (commas; semicolons when items contain commas)
No punctuation between subject and verb
Comma or parenthesis pair around a supplementary element
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
No punctuation between a verb or preposition and its object
Question versus statement (word order and end mark)

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a past-participle opener
items.passage: In 1934, physicist Enrico Fermi claimed that bombarding uranium with neutrons had made elements heavier than uranium. German chemist Ida Noddack offered a different explanation: the nuclei might have split into a few large ______ ignored by other scientists at the time, her idea anticipated the discovery of fission by four years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “the nuclei might have split into a few large fragments.” The next sentence opens with the phrase “Largely ignored by other scientists at the time,” which describes that sentence’s subject, “her idea,” and is followed by the main verb “anticipated.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: With a comma, “largely ignored by other scientists at the time” seems to describe the fragments, and the main clause “her idea anticipated the discovery ...” is then joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “fragments largely ignored by other scientists” keeps the phrase in the first sentence, and the main clause “her idea anticipated ...” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “That were largely ignored ...” turns the phrase into a description of the fragments inside the first sentence, so the main clause “her idea anticipated ...” is still attached to it with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: science (Ida Noddack’s 1934 critique of Fermi’s transuranium claim, suggesting the nucleus breaks into large fragments; fission found by Hahn and Strassmann in December 1938). Band 6: opener of 7 words, a past participle that reads naturally on “fragments”; menu of 3.20 (essays, praising / essays and praising / essays praising / essays. Praising) with a that-were option instead of and. A colon earlier in the same sentence is structure to parse, not tested.

band7.why: Band-6 S1_period shape (3.20 menu with a that-were form): 7-word participial opener that can hang on “fragments,” splice visible at “her idea” 8 words on; short of band 7's longer opener and run.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before an -ing opener
items.passage: In 1929, crystallographer Kathleen Lonsdale settled a long debate among chemists when she used X-rays to study crystals of hexamethylbenzene, a compound built around a benzene ______ the position of each carbon atom precisely, she demonstrated that the ring is flat rather than puckered.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence is complete at “a compound built around a benzene ring.” The next sentence opens with the participial phrase “Mapping the position of each carbon atom precisely,” which describes its subject, “she,” and is followed by the main verb “demonstrated.” A period is needed between the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma attaches “mapping the position of each carbon atom” to the first main clause, so the second main clause, “she demonstrated that the ring is flat ...,” is joined to it with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “And mapping” tries to join the phrase to the first sentence, but it is not parallel with “used” or “study,” and the main clause “she demonstrated ...” still follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no mark, “a benzene ring mapping the position of each carbon atom” keeps the phrase in the first sentence, and the main clause “she demonstrated ...” is then joined with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: science (Kathleen Lonsdale, 1929 X-ray study of hexamethylbenzene showing the benzene ring is planar). Band 6: -ing opener of 8 words; one-sentence run of 45 words; and-version as in 3.20 (essays and praising) and 886dc9f9 (Bay and having).

band7.why: 8-word -ing opener that reads as a trailing modifier of “used X-rays” until “she demonstrated” (3.20, 886dc9f9 menu); a band-6 target, met.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long past-participle opener
items.passage: Most ancient Greek music survives only in fragments, but one song was preserved in its entirety on a marble ______ above each syllable with symbols indicating pitch and rhythm, the song, known as the Seikilos epitaph and presumably composed in the first century CE, is the oldest complete musical composition yet discovered.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence is complete at “one song was preserved in its entirety on a marble column.” The second sentence opens with the participial phrase “Marked above each syllable with symbols indicating pitch and rhythm,” which describes its subject, “the song,” and the main verb “is” follows the comma-set phrase “known as the Seikilos epitaph and presumably composed in the first century CE.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “a marble column marked above each syllable ...” keeps the phrase in the first sentence as a description of the column, and the main clause “the song ... is the oldest complete musical composition” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: The comma also lets the phrase describe the column, so the main clause “the song ... is the oldest complete musical composition yet discovered” is joined to the first sentence with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “That was marked ...” makes the phrase a relative clause about the column inside the first sentence, so the main clause “the song ... is ...” is still joined to it with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: history and music (Seikilos epitaph, marble column found near Aydın, Turkey, about the first century CE). Band-7 checks (band7/boundaries.md section 6): opener 10 words and attachable to “column”; cue outside a 6-word window; run 51 words; reasoning steps 3 to 4. Option menu of a872c60a (tenets. Developed / tenets developed / tenets that, developed / tenets, developed) with a that-was form. No logic-wrong distractor (the template’s band-7 models have none).
band7_moves: opener of 10 words, a past participle that reads naturally on clause 1’s last noun (a column marked with signs)
clause 2’s subject is followed by a comma-set phrase of 13 words, so the splice shows only at “is,” 26 words after the blank
one-sentence run of 51 words; clause 1 is itself a compound sentence joined by “but”

band7.why: 10-word past-participle opener that hangs on “column” (a column marked with symbols), then a 13-word comma-set phrase after “the song,” so the splice shows only at “is” (a872c60a, ba8ebf49 shape); comma, glued and that-was options all fail far from the blank.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening the second clause (rather)
items.passage: Cherokee playwright Lynn Riggs’s Green Grow the Lilacs, a 1931 drama set in Indian Territory, closed after a disappointingly brief Broadway engagement. The play did not simply fade ______ it lives on through Oklahoma!, the enormously successful 1943 musical that Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein II adapted from Riggs’s script.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The play did not simply fade away” and “it lives on through Oklahoma! ...” are both main clauses, so a semicolon belongs between them. “Rather” introduces the second clause, which offers the alternative to the denied idea, so it follows the semicolon and is set off with a comma.

A.why_wrong: Commas on both sides of “rather” leave the two main clauses, “The play did not simply fade away” and “it lives on through Oklahoma! ...,” joined by commas alone, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: Nothing separates “fade away” from “rather,” so the first main clause runs straight into the second without the semicolon or period that two main clauses need.

D.why_wrong: This places “rather” at the end of the first clause, where it has no sensible meaning; “rather” must begin the second clause to introduce the alternative to fading away.

items.notes: Subject: literature and theater (Lynn Riggs, Green Grow the Lilacs, 1931, adapted as Oklahoma!, 1943). Band 6: not X; rather, Y as in 3.5 (novel; rather,); menu of 2.8 (ones, even so; / ones even so, / ones; even so, / ones, even so,). Titles would be italic in print.

band7.why: not X; rather, Y as in 3.5; the negation “did not simply” sits next to the blank, so the cue is local, and band 7 never uses rather; a band-6 target, met.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing the first clause (however), second clause explains
items.passage: Astrophysicist Jedidah Isler studies blazars, galaxies whose central black holes fire jets of particles almost directly toward Earth, making them look extremely bright. That brightness is partly ______ because a jet’s light is concentrated in the direction it travels, a blazar seen head-on looks far brighter than it would from any other angle.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “That brightness is partly deceptive” qualifies the previous sentence’s point that blazars “look extremely bright,” so “however” belongs at the end of this first clause, set off by a comma. The second main clause, “because a jet’s light is concentrated ..., a blazar seen head-on looks far brighter ...,” explains why the brightness is deceptive, and a semicolon correctly separates the two clauses.

B.why_wrong: Putting “however” at the start of the second clause signals a contrast between the clauses, but the second clause explains the first rather than contrasting with it; the contrast is with the previous sentence.

C.why_wrong: With commas on both sides of “however,” the “because” clause can attach to the first clause, but the main clause “a blazar seen head-on looks far brighter ...” is then joined with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the two main clauses run together; there is no semicolon or period between “deceptive however” and the second clause.

items.notes: Subject: science (Jedidah Isler studies blazars; relativistic beaming makes a jet aimed at Earth look brighter). Band-7 checks: logic-wrong distractor present; cue (the previous sentence’s claim) outside a 6-word window; subordinate-clause opener for clause 2 as in a05cc490; menu of 5aa171de (pristine, though / pristine, though; / pristine; though / pristine, though,) with however.
band7_moves: clause 1 qualifies the previous sentence (“extremely bright” then “partly deceptive”), so the adverb closes clause 1
logic-wrong distractor “; however,” that is grammatical but sets up a false contrast with an explaining clause
clause 2 opens with a subordinate “because” clause, so the comma-pair version hides its splice until “a blazar seen head-on,” 13 words past the blank

band7.why: Adverb closes clause 1, which qualifies the previous sentence's “look extremely bright” (21e58a83, be37d4ae); clause 2 opens with a because-clause, so the comma-pair splice shows 13 words on. The “; however,” trap is grammatical but wrong by meaning: clause 2 gives the reason clause 1 is true (beaming makes a head-on blazar look brighter than it would from any other angle), so it cannot contrast with it; a careful student who asks what “however” contrasts finds only the previous sentence.

review.note: batch note: “; however,” confirmed wrong by meaning (clause 2 explains clause 1, no contrast); see band7.why

items.subtype: Restrictive appositive: descriptor and name, followed by dates
items.passage: Woodcuts depicting traditional life on the windswept mountain plateaus of Finnmark, Norway’s northernmost region, are now preserved in national collections, yet their creator often sold them door to door for almost nothing. Throughout his brief career, Norwegian Sámi ______ (1902–1938) exhibited his prints only three times.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Norwegian Sámi artist” is a descriptor with no article that works like a title before the name “John Savio,” so the name is essential and takes no commas. The dates in parentheses belong to the name, and no comma may come between the subject and its verb, “exhibited.”

A.why_wrong: The commas treat “John Savio” as extra information, but without an article “Norwegian Sámi artist” cannot stand alone as the subject; the name is essential and must not be set off.

B.why_wrong: The comma after the name separates the subject, “Norwegian Sámi artist John Savio (1902–1938),” from its verb, “exhibited.”

C.why_wrong: The comma splits the descriptor “Norwegian Sámi artist” from the name it identifies, and no comma follows to close an interruption.

items.notes: Subject: arts (John Savio, 1902 to 1938, Sámi woodcut artist from Finnmark who sold his prints door to door and had three exhibitions, two in Tromsø and one in Paris; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Savio). Reviewer replaced the writer's Hisaye Yamamoto subject: a Japanese American woman writer contrasting two generations with the same 2 x 2 menu cloned official 6d4b2e1e (Wakako Yamauchi). Band-7 checks: S4_restrictive is exempt from the local-window check; comma-tempting material (dates, verb) after the name as in fa36d803 (artist Marie-Denise Villers (1774–1821)); first mention of the name at the blank.
band7_moves: descriptor plus name followed by dates in parentheses and then the verb, so a closing comma looks natural
options cross comma before the name with comma after it (2 x 2), as in 0a114526 and 6d4b2e1e
the man is introduced only as “their creator” before the blank, so the name is new information at the blank

band7.why: Descriptor plus name, then dates and the verb, 2 x 2 comma menu as in 6d4b2e1e and 0a114526; dates after the name tempt a closing comma as in fa36d803.

fixes: replaced the subject (Hisaye Yamamoto, a Japanese American woman writer contrasting two generations, with the same 2 x 2 menu, cloned official 6d4b2e1e on Wakako Yamauchi) with John Savio, Sámi woodcut artist; new passage, options, explanation and distractors; claimed in claims.txt and Yamamoto withdrawn

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase that specifies it
items.passage: Some societies punish minor breaches of custom that others readily tolerate. In a 2011 study spanning thirty-three nations, psychologist Michele Gelfand and her colleagues evaluated each culture on a single ______ tightness, or the strength of the social norms that its members are expected to observe and the severity of the penalties for violating them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Psychologist Michele Gelfand and her colleagues evaluated each culture on a single scale” is a complete main clause, and what follows, “its tightness, or the strength of the social norms ... and the severity of the penalties ...,” is a noun phrase that names that scale. A colon correctly introduces a phrase that specifies something announced in the main clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “its tightness, or the strength of the social norms ...” has no main verb of its own; “are expected” belongs to the clause that describes the norms.

B.why_wrong: The period leaves “Its tightness, or the strength of the social norms that its members are expected to observe ...” as a sentence fragment, since the noun phrase has no main verb.

D.why_wrong: Adding “it was” makes the noun phrase a main clause, but that clause is then joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: social science (Gelfand et al. 2011, tight and loose cultures across 33 nations; tightness defined as the strength of norms and the tolerance of deviance). Band-7 checks: colon key after an announcing noun; the fragment cue (no main verb) is spread over the 24 words after the blank; reasoning steps 3.
band7_moves: announcing noun (“a single scale”) followed by a noun phrase whose relative clause carries a finite verb (“that its members are expected to observe”), so the semicolon and period fragments can pass a quick look
menu of 3.18 (extensive: a / extensive; a / extensive, it was a / extensive. A)
run of 43 words after an 11-word context sentence; no lone-dash option

band7.why: Announcing noun (“a single scale”) then a noun phrase whose relative clause carries a finite verb (“are expected”), so the semicolon and period fragments pass a quick read; e9aee0d8 menu with “it was its” splice.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before the item it names
items.passage: Harvard mycologist Roland Thaxter spent decades describing hundreds of species of Laboulbeniales, fungi so minuscule that they are seldom noticed without a microscope and so specialized that they flourish on only one kind of ______ the hardened outer shells of living insects and other arthropods.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “they flourish on only one kind of surface” is complete and announces something it does not yet name. A colon correctly introduces the noun phrase that names it, “the hardened outer shells of living insects and other arthropods.”

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “the hardened outer shells of living insects and other arthropods” is a noun phrase with no verb.

C.why_wrong: The period leaves “The hardened outer shells of living insects and other arthropods” as a sentence fragment.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “one kind of surface the hardened outer shells ...” runs two noun phrases together; a colon is needed to introduce the phrase that names the surface.

items.notes: Subject: science (Roland Thaxter’s monograph on the Laboulbeniales, fungi that live on the exoskeletons of insects and other arthropods). Band 6: one-sentence run of 44 words; menu of 3.22 (plant. / plant; / plant / plant:).

band7.why: Colon after an announcing noun before a plain noun phrase with no finite verb, as 3.22; the fragments are easy to spot, so band 6, as targeted.

items.subtype: Closing a dash pair around an element that holds its own comma-set appositive
items.passage: Mesoamerican priests consulted a 260-day ritual calendar to choose favorable days for weddings, journeys, and other undertakings. The Codex Borgia—a screenfold manuscript painted on deer hide and named for ______ is among the most richly illustrated guides to that calendar to survive from before the Spanish conquest.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Stefano Borgia, the cardinal who once owned it—
Stefano Borgia—the cardinal who once owned it,
Stefano Borgia, the cardinal who once owned it,
Stefano Borgia: the cardinal who once owned it—
items.explanation: The dash after “The Codex Borgia” opens a supplementary element, so a second dash must close it before the main verb “is.” Inside that element, “the cardinal who once owned it” is an appositive renaming Stefano Borgia, set off by a comma before it; the closing dash also ends that appositive.

B.why_wrong: The dash after “Borgia” closes the dash element too early, leaving “the cardinal who once owned it,” stranded between the element and the verb “is.”

C.why_wrong: The comma can close the appositive “the cardinal who once owned it,” but the dash pair opened after “The Codex Borgia” is never closed, so the element runs into the main clause.

D.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause, but “a screenfold manuscript painted on deer hide and named for Stefano Borgia” is a noun phrase inside the dash element.

items.notes: Subject: history (Codex Borgia, pre-conquest Mesoamerican divinatory screenfold on animal hide, named for Cardinal Stefano Borgia, 1731 to 1804; tonalpohualli). Band-7 checks: cue (the opening dash) outside a 6-word window; two slots in each option as in 6e071432; reasoning steps 3. Codex title in roman type as in CB passages.
band7_moves: second level inside the dash element: an appositive set off by a comma, so the comma version closes the inner element but not the dash pair
partner dash 10 words before the blank; options mix the two levels in both slots
colon option inside the element as a third trap

band7.why: Opening dash 10 words before the blank and an inner comma-set appositive, options mixing the two levels in both slots (6e071432, 109d5bbb); in a 6-word window the comma-pair option looks right.

items.subtype: Semicolons between series items that contain commas
items.passage: Harlem Renaissance painter Aaron Douglas produced covers for The Crisis, the influential magazine of the ______ James Weldon Johnson’s 1927 collection of verse sermons; and Aspects of Negro Life, a sequence of monumental murals commissioned in 1934 for a branch of the New York Public Library.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three works, and each item carries its own comma-set description, so semicolons must separate the items, as the semicolon after “verse sermons” shows. A semicolon ends the first item after “the NAACP,” and a comma sets off the description of God’s Trombones, “James Weldon Johnson’s 1927 collection of verse sermons.”

A.why_wrong: A comma after “NAACP” does not match the semicolon used later in the list, and it makes “illustrations for God’s Trombones” read as part of the description of The Crisis.

B.why_wrong: The semicolon is right, but without a comma after “God’s Trombones,” the title runs into its own description, “James Weldon Johnson’s 1927 collection of verse sermons.”

D.why_wrong: A colon cannot separate two items of a list; “covers for The Crisis, the influential magazine of the NAACP” does not introduce what follows.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Aaron Douglas: covers for The Crisis, illustrations for God’s Trombones, 1927, and the 1934 murals Aspects of Negro Life for the 135th Street branch). Band 6: two slots per option as in 3.23 (Lagos; A Kind of Marriage,); one-sentence run of 45 words. Titles would be italic in print.

band7.why: Complex series with the revealing semicolon after the blank (“sermons; and”), two slots as in 3.23; no second rule inside the option, which band 7 adds; a band-6 target, met.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a long subject and its verb
items.passage: Song dynasty poet Li Qingzhao is celebrated chiefly for her ci, lyrics composed to fit existing melodies. The afterword she wrote for her late husband’s catalog of the bronze and stone inscriptions the couple had spent decades ______ also deserves recognition as a remarkably candid memoir describing how most of their collection was lost during wartime.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the long noun phrase “The afterword she wrote for her late husband’s catalog of the bronze and stone inscriptions the couple had spent decades collecting,” and its verb is “deserves.” No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb.

A.why_wrong: The comma separates the long subject, which ends at “collecting,” from its verb, “deserves”; no comma was opened earlier that this one could close.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but the words before it are only a subject without a verb, and the words after it lack a subject.

C.why_wrong: A single dash has no role here: nothing is being set off, and the dash splits the subject from its verb, “deserves.”

items.notes: Subject: literature (Li Qingzhao’s afterword to Zhao Mingcheng’s Records on Metal and Stone, the couple’s collection lost after the Jurchen invasion). Band 6: 21-word subject with no comma in it and an earlier comma-set appositive in the first sentence; the subject starts 20 words before the blank.

band7.why: S4_subj_verb has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6: 21-word subject with no internal comma begun 20 words before the blank.

items.subtype: Comma pair around an interrupter after a conjunction
items.passage: According to physicist Kenneth Libbrecht, the ice spikes that occasionally rise from ice cube trays form when freezing water seals its surface except for a small hole. The expanding ice underneath then forces water up through that hole, where it freezes along the perimeter ______ builds a hollow tube that can grow several centimeters tall.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Over time” is an interrupter inside the compound predicate “freezes along the perimeter and ... builds a hollow tube,” so it must be set off by a pair of commas, one before it and one after it.

A.why_wrong: The comma after “over time” has no partner before it, so the interrupter is closed but never opened.

C.why_wrong: A single dash after “over time” has no partner and no role; it splits the verb “builds” from the rest of the compound predicate.

D.why_wrong: The comma before “over time” opens the interrupter, but no comma closes it before “builds.”

items.notes: Subject: science (ice spikes in freezer trays, Kenneth Libbrecht’s experiments; water pushed up through a hole in the frozen surface freezes around its edge). Band 6: the one hard comma-pair model 3.12 (and, in the process,) with its menu; the and-clause sits inside a where-clause, so the student must see the compound predicate.

band7.why: S3_comma_pair has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 on the one hard model 3.12 and its menu, with the compound predicate hidden inside a where-clause.

items.subtype: Comma plus and between two independent clauses
items.passage: Dura-Europos, a Roman frontier town overlooking the Euphrates in present-day Syria, was abandoned after a Sasanian army captured it around 256 CE. Its ruins lay buried beneath windblown sand for nearly seventeen ______ excavations in the 1920s and 1930s uncovered a synagogue whose walls are decorated with painted biblical scenes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Its ruins lay buried beneath windblown sand for nearly seventeen centuries” and “excavations in the 1920s and 1930s uncovered a synagogue ...” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together as a fused sentence.

B.why_wrong: When “and” joins two main clauses this long, a comma is needed before it.

D.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses; without a conjunction it creates a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Dura-Europos, taken by the Sasanians about 256 CE, excavated by Yale and the French Academy 1928 to 1937; synagogue frescoes). Menu of 2.2 (1680 / 1680 and / 1680, / 1680, and).

items.subtype: Closing a comma pair around an appositive
items.passage: The Prix de Rome, a prestigious French scholarship that sent promising young artists to study in Italy, had been awarded for musical composition since 1803. Lili Boulanger, a nineteen-year-old composer whose cantata Faust et Hélène won the prize in ______ became the first woman to receive it for composition.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The comma after “Boulanger” opens the appositive “a nineteen-year-old composer whose cantata Faust et Hélène won the prize in 1913,” which describes the subject, “Lili Boulanger.” A second comma must close the appositive before the verb “became.”

B.why_wrong: Without a comma after “1913,” the appositive opened after “Boulanger” is never closed, and its last words run straight into the verb “became.”

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but the words before it are a subject and its appositive with no main verb.

D.why_wrong: The appositive is opened with a comma, so it must be closed with a comma, not a dash.

items.notes: Subject: arts and music (Lili Boulanger, first woman to win the Prix de Rome for composition, 1913, cantata Faust et Hélène; music prize from 1803). Reviewer moved the name to the front: in the draft (“The first woman to win in that category, nineteen-year-old composer Lili ______ triumphed”) the no-comma option read as a fronted appositive plus subject, a second defensible answer. Partner comma 13 words before the blank, as 7f48b098. Title would be italic in print.

fixes: second defensible option: B (“The first woman to win in that category, nineteen-year-old composer Lili Boulanger triumphed”) is a legal fronted appositive; rewrote sentence 2 so the name comes first and the blank closes the appositive (“won the prize in 1913, became”); options now 1913 variants

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a short introductory phrase
items.passage: In the fifth century BCE, the Nile island of Elephantine was home to a garrison of Jewish soldiers who guarded Egypt’s southern frontier on behalf of the Persian ______ a letter composed in Aramaic around 407 BCE, the community’s leaders appealed to the governor of Judah for assistance in rebuilding their temple.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence is complete at “on behalf of the Persian Empire.” The second sentence begins with the introductory phrase “In a letter composed in Aramaic around 407 BCE,” followed by its subject, “the community’s leaders,” and verb, “appealed.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma leaves the two main clauses, “the Nile island of Elephantine was home to ...” and “the community’s leaders appealed ...,” joined by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “in a letter composed in Aramaic” attaches to the first sentence, and the second main clause, “the community’s leaders appealed ...,” then follows with only a comma.

C.why_wrong: “Which” begins a relative clause that is never completed: “which in a letter ... , the community’s leaders appealed” is not grammatical.

items.notes: Subject: history (Elephantine papyri: the Jewish garrison under Persian rule; the 407 BCE petition in Aramaic to Bagohi, governor of Judah, about rebuilding the temple destroyed in 410 BCE). Medium: opener of 9 words beginning with In, as 2.10 (earlier. In / earlier, in / earlier, which in / earlier in).

items.subtype: Closing a dash pair around an appositive
items.passage: Ukrainian-born French artist Sonia Delaunay is known for paintings, textiles, and clothing filled with circles and blocks of contrasting color. A crib quilt that she sewed for her son in 1911—a patchwork of brightly colored scraps arranged in loose geometric ______ is often regarded as the starting point of that style.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “1911” opens an appositive describing the quilt, “a patchwork of brightly colored scraps arranged in loose geometric shapes.” A second dash must close it before the verb “is.”

A.why_wrong: The element was opened with a dash, so it must be closed with a dash, not a comma.

C.why_wrong: Without a closing dash, the appositive opened after “1911” runs straight into the verb “is.”

D.why_wrong: Adding “and” treats “is often regarded ...” as a second verb joined to something in the appositive, and the dash element is still never closed.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Sonia Delaunay’s 1911 patchwork quilt for her son, seen as the start of her abstract, color-contrast work). Partner dash 10 words before the blank.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a long subject and its verb
items.passage: In a 1929 paper, economist Harold Hotelling imagined two shops selling identical goods along a single street. His conclusion that the competing shopkeepers would end up side by side at the street’s ______ has since been used to explain why rival businesses often cluster together and why opposing political parties drift toward similar positions.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is “His conclusion that the competing shopkeepers would end up side by side at the street’s midpoint,” and its verb is “has since been used.” No punctuation should come between a subject and its verb.

A.why_wrong: The comma separates the long subject from its verb, “has since been used.”

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but the words before it are a subject with no verb.

D.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause, and “His conclusion that ... at the street’s midpoint” is only the subject of the sentence.

items.notes: Subject: social science (Harold Hotelling, “Stability in Competition,” 1929; clustering of sellers and of party positions). Medium: a 16-word subject ending in a that-clause before the verb, as 2.11 (the reason ... while falling is).

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before an explanation
items.passage: Many Confucian scholars of the Ming dynasty maintained, following the earlier philosopher Zhu Xi, that a person must first learn what is right and only then act on it. Philosopher Wang Yangming rejected this assumption, teaching something ______ unity of knowing and acting, a principle holding that knowledge never translated into action is not genuine knowledge.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Philosopher Wang Yangming rejected this assumption, teaching something different” is a complete main clause that announces an idea it does not yet name. A colon correctly introduces the noun phrase that names it, “the unity of knowing and acting, a principle holding that knowledge never translated into action is not genuine knowledge.”

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “the unity of knowing and acting, a principle holding that ...” is a noun phrase with no main verb; “is” belongs to the that-clause inside it.

C.why_wrong: A colon cannot come between the article “the” and the noun phrase it begins, “unity of knowing and acting.”

D.why_wrong: The period leaves “The unity of knowing and acting, a principle holding that knowledge never translated into action is not genuine knowledge” as a sentence fragment with no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: philosophy (Wang Yangming, 1472 to 1529, unity of knowledge and action, against the view that knowledge precedes action). Menu of 2.15 (new: sequencing / new; sequencing / new, sequencing: / new. Sequencing).

review.note: batch note: no second option; B and D leave a verbless fragment (“holding” is a participle, “is” belongs to the that-clause), C puts the colon after “the”

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: Geologist Florence Bascom specialized in crystalline rocks, which she studied for decades in the hills of Pennsylvania and Maryland. In 1896, she became the first woman hired ______ the United States Geological Survey, the federal agency that studies the nation’s landscapes and natural resources.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The United States Geological Survey” is the object of the preposition “by,” and no punctuation should separate a preposition from its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause; “she became the first woman hired by” is incomplete without its object.

B.why_wrong: The comma separates the preposition “by” from its object, “the United States Geological Survey.”

C.why_wrong: A dash has no role between “by” and its object; nothing here is being set off.

items.notes: Subject: science (Florence Bascom, first woman hired by the USGS, 1896; Piedmont crystalline rocks). Menu of 1.21 (by; / by: / by, / by) with a dash for the semicolon.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its object
items.passage: Tektites are small fragments of natural glass that form when a large meteorite strikes Earth and melted rock is flung high into the atmosphere. Tektites from a single impact approximately 790,000 years ago are scattered across an area that ______ much of Southeast Asia and Australia.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Much of Southeast Asia and Australia” is the object of the verb “covers,” and no punctuation should separate a verb from its object.

A.why_wrong: The comma separates the verb “covers” from its object, “much of Southeast Asia and Australia.”

C.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause, but “an area that covers” is incomplete without its object.

D.why_wrong: A dash has no role between “covers” and its object; nothing here is being set off.

items.notes: Subject: science (Australasian tektite strewn field, impact about 790,000 years ago). Menu of 1.16 (colon, comma, dash and no mark after the verb).

items.subtype: Embedded question: statement order and a period
items.passage: Ninth-century Baghdad scholar al-Kindi wrote the earliest known description of frequency analysis, a technique for deciphering coded messages. First, a sample of ordinary writing is examined to determine how often ______ Then the most frequent symbols in a coded message are matched with the most frequent letters.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “How often each letter appears” is an embedded question: it is part of a statement and serves as the object of “determine.” An embedded question keeps statement word order (subject “each letter,” then verb “appears”), and the sentence, being a statement, ends with a period.

A.why_wrong: The inverted order “does each letter appear” and the question mark belong to a direct question, but the sentence is a statement that contains an embedded question.

B.why_wrong: The word order is right, but the sentence is a statement, so it should end with a period, not a question mark.

D.why_wrong: An embedded question takes statement order, so “does each letter appear” is wrong even though the sentence correctly ends with a period.

items.notes: Subject: history of science (al-Kindi, ninth-century Baghdad, earliest known account of frequency analysis in his treatise on deciphering coded messages). Statement-order key as in 1.7 (most people prefer in a diet drink.).

items.subtype: Comma plus but between two independent clauses
items.passage: Japanese psychiatrist Tamaki Saitō popularized the word hikikomori to describe people who remain at home for six months or longer, avoiding school, work, and friends. The condition was once thought to exist only in ______ cases have since been reported in South Korea, Spain, and the United States.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The condition was once thought to exist only in Japan” and “cases have since been reported in South Korea, Spain, and the United States” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them and signals the contrast.

B.why_wrong: When “but” joins two main clauses like these, a comma is needed before it.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two main clauses; without a conjunction it creates a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together as a fused sentence.

items.notes: Subject: social science (hikikomori, popularized by Tamaki Saitō’s 1998 book; reports outside Japan). Menu of 1.27 (time but / time, but / time, / time).

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory phrase
items.passage: Indian artist Nalini Malani is celebrated for installations that she calls video/shadow plays. After painting figures on the inside of large transparent plastic ______ Malani sets them rotating in a darkened gallery, where lamps and video projectors cast their moving shadows across the surrounding walls.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “After painting figures on the inside of large transparent plastic cylinders” is an introductory phrase that comes before the main clause, “Malani sets them rotating in a darkened gallery.” A comma correctly separates the introductory phrase from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: Without a comma, the introductory phrase runs into the main clause, so “cylinders Malani” reads as one unit.

B.why_wrong: The period leaves “After painting figures on the inside of large transparent plastic cylinders” as a sentence fragment.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but the words before it are an introductory phrase that cannot stand alone.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Nalini Malani’s video/shadow plays with rotating reverse-painted Mylar cylinders). Menu of 1.19 (classroom. / classroom; / classroom, / classroom).

items.subtype: Commas between items of a simple series
items.passage: South African chemist Tebello Nyokong studies dyes called phthalocyanines for use in photodynamic cancer therapy. In this treatment, a dye is injected into the ______ accumulates in tumor cells, and releases a toxic form of oxygen when it is exposed to light.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three things the dye does: it “is injected into the body,” “accumulates in tumor cells,” and “releases a toxic form of oxygen.” A comma correctly separates the first item from the second, matching the comma after “cells.”

A.why_wrong: Semicolons separate list items only when the items contain commas; these simple verb phrases need commas, as the comma after “cells” shows.

B.why_wrong: A colon cannot separate two items in a list; “a dye is injected into the body” does not introduce what follows.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, “the body accumulates in tumor cells” reads as if the body were the subject of “accumulates.”

items.notes: Subject: science (Tebello Nyokong, Rhodes University, phthalocyanine photosensitizers for photodynamic therapy). Menu of 1.12 (themselves; / themselves, / themselves. And / themselves) with a colon.

items.subtype: Comma before a nonrestrictive which clause
items.passage: Ciudad Perdida, an ancient city in the mountains of northern Colombia, was built by the Tairona people beginning around 800 CE. The city spreads across more than 160 stone ______ once supported houses and are connected by a network of paths and staircases.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause ends with “The city spreads across more than 160 stone terraces.” What follows, “which once supported houses and are connected by a network of paths and staircases,” is a nonrestrictive relative clause that adds information about the terraces, and a comma correctly separates it from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “which once supported houses ...” is a relative clause that cannot stand alone.

C.why_wrong: The period leaves “Which once supported houses and are connected by a network of paths and staircases” as a sentence fragment.

D.why_wrong: Without “which,” the verbs “supported” and “are connected” have no link to the main clause: “The city spreads across more than 160 stone terraces once supported houses” is not grammatical.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Ciudad Perdida, or Teyuna, Tairona city in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, begun about 800 CE, 169 terraces). Menu of 1.32 (Act, which / Act; which / Act. Which / Act).
